title: Hello World
description: Write a function that returns the text `Hello World`.

title: Sum Two Numbers
description: Return the sum of two integers.

title: Your First Program
description:
Write a function called `greet` that says hello to whoever's name it's given. `greet("Ada")` should give back `Hello, Ada!`

New to coding? Replace `pass` (or the empty line between the `{ }`) with:

`return "Hello, " + name + "!"`

In Java, C#, C++, JavaScript and TypeScript, put a `;` at the end of that line.

title: FizzBuzz
description:
Count from `1` to `n` and return every step as text in a list. For multiples of **3**, use `Fizz` instead of the number. For multiples of **5**, use `Buzz`. For multiples of **both 3 and 5**, use `FizzBuzz`.

`fizzBuzz(5)` returns `["1", "2", "Fizz", "4", "Buzz"]`.

`n` is between 1 and 100.

title: Bubble Sort Swap Counter
description:
Bubble sort sorts a list by repeatedly swapping neighbours that are in the wrong order. Return **how many swaps** bubble sort would make to sort `nums` from smallest to largest. Equal numbers are never swapped.

`countSwaps([3, 1, 2])` returns `2`: swap 3 and 1, then swap 3 and 2.

The catch: the hidden tests use lists of **20,000 numbers**, and really running bubble sort on those is far too slow. Find a faster way to count. Hint: every swap fixes exactly one pair of positions `i < j` where `nums[i] > nums[j]`. How could merge sort count those pairs while it sorts?

`nums` has up to 20,000 numbers between -100,000 and 100,000. The count is returned as a `long`, because on longer lists it can grow past what an `int` holds.

title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
description:
Convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit using the formula **F = C × 9 / 5 + 32**.

`celsiusToFahrenheit(100)` returns `212.0`.

Watch your data types! In Java, C# and C++, `9 / 5` is integer division and gives `1`, not `1.8`. Write `9.0 / 5` so the math stays a decimal (a `double`).

title: Second Largest
description:
Return the **second largest different value** in `nums`. Repeats of the largest value don't count.

`secondLargest([4, 9, 9, 2])` returns `4`.

There are always at least two different values. Bonus: can you do it in one pass through the list, without sorting?

`nums` has up to 5,000 numbers, and any `int` value is possible.

title: Count the Islands
description:
A map is given as a list of rows, where `#` is land and `.` is water. Land squares that touch **up, down, left or right** (not diagonally) belong to the same island. Return how many islands there are.

`countIslands(["##...", "##...", "..#..", "...##"])` returns `3`.

Hint: when you find land you haven't visited yet, count a new island, then visit everything connected to it (flood fill) so you don't count it again.

The map has 1 to 60 rows, every row is the same length (1 to 60 characters), and it only contains `#` and `.`.

title: Format the Runtime
description:
A movie app prints how long a movie is like `2h 5m`. Given the length in minutes, return the text exactly as it should be printed: the hours, `h`, a space, the leftover minutes, then `m`.

`formatMinutes(125)` returns `2h 5m`.

You'll need integer division (`/`, or `//` in Python) for the hours and the remainder operator `%` for the minutes. In Python, turn numbers into text with `str()` before joining them to other text.

`totalMinutes` is between 0 and 10,000.

title: Palindrome Check
description:
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like `racecar`. Return `true` if `text` is a palindrome **when you ignore capital letters, spaces and punctuation** (only letters and digits count). Otherwise return `false`.

Text with no letters or digits at all (including empty text) counts as a palindrome.

`text` uses plain English characters and can be up to 20,000 characters long.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

title: Balanced Parentheses
description:
Return **every** balanced string you can make from `n` pairs of parentheses, in any order. Balanced means every `(` is closed by a `)` that comes after it, and no `)` appears before its matching `(`.

`generateParentheses(2)` returns `["(())", "()()"]`.

This is a backtracking problem, like N-Queens: build the string one character at a time, and only add a character when the string can still end up balanced.

`n` is between 1 and 8.

title: camelCase Names
description:
Java, C# and JavaScript name variables in **camelCase**: the first word is all lowercase, and each word after it starts with a capital letter, like `playerScore` or `firstName`.

Given two words, join them into a camelCase name. The words can arrive in any mix of capital and lowercase letters, so fix them up.

`toCamelCase("PLAYER", "score")` returns `playerScore`.

Each word has at least one letter and contains only letters.

title: Run-Length Encoding
description:
Run-length encoding shrinks text by replacing each run of the same character with that character followed by how many times it repeats in a row.

`compress("aaabcc")` returns `a3b1c2`.

Capital and lowercase letters are different characters, and runs of 10 or more just use the full number (`a12`). Empty text gives back empty text.

`text` can be up to 10,000 characters long.

title: Fewest Coins
description:
Return the **fewest coins** that add up to exactly `amount`, using as many of each coin value as you like. If it can't be done, return `-1`.

`minCoins([1, 3, 4], 6)` returns `2` (3 + 3).

Careful: always grabbing the biggest coin doesn't work. For that example it picks 4 + 1 + 1, which is 3 coins. Trying every combination is too slow for the hidden tests too. Think about building up the answer for every amount from 0 to `amount`.

There are 1 to 12 different coin values, each between 1 and 1,000, and `amount` is between 0 and 10,000.
